essays.text:
If schools are going to make us do projects over the summer, then those projects should be designed by the students, not handed to us by a teacher in June with a due date in August. I understand why teachers want to assign something. They don't want us to forget everything we learned. But a project you didn't choose is a project you do the night before, and nobody learns anything the night before.

The main reason student-designed projects work better is that summer is not school. During the year I have six classes and a schedule and a bell that tells me where to be. In the summer none of that exists. The only thing that is going to get me to sit down and work on something in July is actually caring about it. Last summer my English teacher assigned a summer reading project where we had to read a novel from a list and write a five paragraph analysis of the main theme. I read the book in two days because I liked it, and then I did not touch the essay until the week before school started. I wrote it fast and I got a B and I could not tell you today what I said in it. That same summer, on my own, I taught myself to edit video because I wanted to make a highlight reel for my cousin's soccer team. Nobody graded that. I spent maybe thirty hours on it. Which one do you think I actually learned from?

People who disagree say students will just pick something easy. That's a fair point, and honestly some kids would. But that's an argument for having rules, not for taking the choice away. A school could say the project has to take at least twenty hours, has to produce something you can show other people, and has to include a short written reflection about what was hard. You send your idea to a teacher in May, the teacher approves it or tells you to make it bigger, and then you go do it. That way the teacher is still involved, but as a coach instead of the person writing the assignment. You still get accountability without pretending that one assignment fits three hundred different people.

There's also the fairness issue that nobody talks about. A teacher-designed project assumes everyone's summer looks the same. It doesn't. Some students work forty hours a week at a job. Some go to their grandparents in another country for six weeks with bad internet. A packet of thirty math problems or a group presentation is way harder for those students than it is for someone sitting home with a laptop and nothing to do. When students design their own project, they can build it around the summer they are actually having. The kid with the job could study something about their workplace. The kid traveling could do something about the place they're going.

I'm not saying summer projects are pointless. Keeping your brain on is a real thing, and I've felt how rusty I am in September. But the way to keep someone's brain on is to let them point it at something they picked. Teachers should set the standards and check the work. Students should decide what the work is.

Every year on the last day of school my teachers hand out the summer packet, which is a strange way of saying have a nice break. I don't actually think summer work is a bad idea. What I think is that students should be the ones designing the projects, with a teacher approving the plan, instead of getting a project that was already finished before they ever saw it.

The biggest reason is that people do the work when the work is theirs. A teacher-designed project has to fit thirty different kids at once, so it turns into the most general assignment possible and nobody's favorite. Last summer my English teacher assigned a reading log, four books off a list with five journal entries each. I read two of them in June, and then I did the other two plus fourteen journal entries in one terrible week in August while my cousins were visiting. Those entries weren't thinking. They were typing. My friend Deniz had a science teacher who let her write her own proposal instead, and she spent almost the whole summer growing tomato plants in different soils because her mom's tomatoes kept dying and she wanted to know why. She was outside measuring things in July. Nobody measures anything in July unless they actually want the answer.

The second reason is that designing a project teaches you something that doing a project doesn't. When you have to decide what your question is, how long it should take, and what counts as being finished, you are learning how real work gets made. Adults don't get handed a rubric when their boss asks them to fix something. My uncle builds kitchen cabinets and he told me the hardest part of any job isn't the cutting, it's figuring out what the customer actually wants before you start. If school only ever gives us the finished instructions, we practice following directions for twelve years and then get surprised when nobody gives us directions anymore.

I know what the argument against this is, because my mom said it when I brought it up. Kids will pick something easy. Some would. If you let me design my own project when I was in seventh grade I would have written three sentences about basketball and called it a summer. But that's an argument for having the teacher approve the plan, not for having the teacher write it. Make us turn in a proposal in May with a real question, a rough schedule, and something we have to show at the end, whether that's a paper or a model or a set of data. The teacher can send it back and say this is too small, try again. That takes way less of a teacher's summer than grading ninety identical reading logs, and it means the student had to think about the project twice, once in May and once all summer.

Teacher-designed projects mostly prove that students can survive a deadline. Student-designed projects prove that students can find something worth knowing and stay with it for two months without anyone watching. Schools say the whole reason for summer work is to keep us learning over the break. If that's the actual goal, then let us pick the thing we're willing to keep learning.

If schools are going to make us do summer projects anyway, they should let students design them. I know that sounds like the answer a student would give just because we want the easy way out, but that is not my reason. My reason is that a project you picked yourself is the only kind you actually finish in June instead of the last week of August.

Last summer my English teacher assigned us a list of four books and a reading journal with two entries per book. I read one book in June, forgot about the journal completely, and then wrote twenty-four entries in three days at the end of August while my mom kept asking why I looked like that. I did not learn anything about those books. I learned how to write a paragraph that sounds like I read something. That is what a teacher-designed project taught me. Meanwhile my friend Dev spent that same summer teaching himself to fix bikes because his own bike broke and he did not want to pay forty dollars for a tune up. By August he was fixing bikes for people in our neighborhood for ten dollars each. Nobody assigned that. Nobody graded it. He still knows how to do it and I still could not tell you the plot of book three.

People who want teacher-designed projects usually say students will just pick something easy, and honestly some will. If you tell a kid to design their own summer project, somebody is going to turn in "I watched a lot of documentaries" and call it research. That is a real problem and I am not going to pretend it isn't. But that is an argument for the teacher setting the rules, not for the teacher picking the topic. A teacher can say the project has to take at least twenty hours, it has to produce something you can show, and you have to check in twice over the summer. Inside those rules, students pick. That way the standard is still high but the subject is actually ours.

The other reason is that summer is the only time we get to find out what we like. During the school year our whole day is decided for us, period by period, bell by bell. If summer is also decided for us then there is literally no point in a year where anybody discovers anything. I did not know I was interested in cooking until a summer when I was bored and started making dinner for my family. If someone had handed me a packet in June I would have been busy with the packet.

There is one thing teachers should keep designing, and that is the part where you have to explain yourself. Whatever you choose, you should have to present it in September and answer questions about it. That keeps people honest and it also means the class gets to hear about twenty-five different things instead of the same four books.

So my position is that summer projects should be student-designed with teacher-set requirements. Teachers should decide how much and how serious. Students should decide what. That is the version where the work actually gets done in July, not in a panic the week before school starts.

Every June my school hands out a packet with the summer assignments in it, and every August I watch people finish those assignments in the parking lot before first period. That is not learning. That is copying. If schools actually want students to keep learning over the break, the projects should be student-designed, with the teacher setting the standards but not the topic.

The main reason is that a summer project only works if somebody cares about it. During the school year there are grades, deadlines, parents asking about PowerSchool, and a teacher standing in front of you. In July none of that exists. The only thing that makes a person open a book in July is wanting to. When my English teacher assigned us a specific novel and a five paragraph response on the theme of isolation, I read about sixty pages and then found a summary online in September. Nobody made me do it, so I did the smallest amount that would pass. But that same summer I taught myself how to fix the brakes on my bike, watched probably forty videos about it, and then ended up rebuilding my neighbor's bike too. Nobody assigned that. If the school had let me count that as my summer project I would have had something real to show, plus I would have actually kept learning, which is supposedly the whole point.

People who argue for teacher-designed projects usually say students will pick something easy. That is fair. Some kid will absolutely propose "watch documentaries" and call it a research project. But the answer to that is not to take the choice away, it is to make students submit a proposal in May and have the teacher approve it. The teacher sets the requirements, like twenty hours of work, a written reflection, and some kind of product at the end. The student picks what the twenty hours are spent on. That way the rigor comes from the teacher and the interest comes from the student, and you get both instead of one.

There is also the problem that a teacher-designed project has to be designed for thirty different people at once, which means it fits almost nobody. My AP US History summer packet was fourteen chapters of outlining. For a kid who already reads history books for fun, it was boring busywork he could do half asleep. For a kid who struggles with reading comprehension and had no teacher available for two months, it was impossible, so he copied someone's outlines the night before. The assignment was too easy and too hard at the same time, which is what happens when one assignment tries to cover a whole roster. A student-designed project stretches each person from wherever they actually are.

The last reason is that designing something yourself is a skill, and honestly it might be more important than whatever content is in the packet. In college and in a job nobody hands you a worksheet. Somebody says here is a problem, figure out what to do about it. Learning how to pick a question, plan out how long it will take, and be honest about whether you actually finished is harder than outlining fourteen chapters, and it is the part school almost never teaches.

I am not saying summer projects should be optional or that students should grade themselves. Teachers should still set the bar, approve the plans, and check the work in September. But the topic belongs to the student. A project you chose is something you might actually finish in July instead of in the parking lot in August.

Almost nobody I know actually likes summer projects, but I don't think that's because students hate learning in July. I think it's because of who gets to decide what the project is. If a school is going to take a piece of somebody's summer, that project should be designed by the student, with a teacher approving the plan and checking in on it. A project you picked yourself is a project you will actually finish, and finishing something is the whole point.

The case for teacher-designed projects is usually about fairness and rigor. If everyone gets the same assignment, everyone does the same amount of work, and nobody can slide by with something easy. Teachers also know the curriculum, so they can assign work that lines up with what's coming in the fall. That sounds reasonable on paper. In practice, though, what it produces is packets. My AP US History summer assignment last year was outlining the first six chapters of the textbook. I did all six. I cannot tell you one thing that was in chapter three. I copied headings, turned bold words into bullet points, and my hand hurt. That is not rigor, that's just volume, and the only skill it built was the skill of getting through something.

A student-designed project fixes the motivation problem, which is the real problem. When you choose the thing, you have a reason to keep going when it gets boring, because it was your idea and quitting feels worse. My friend Devin spent last summer teaching himself enough Python to build a program that tracks his fantasy basketball league, and he complained about bugs in that thing for two months straight but never once stopped working on it. No teacher could have assigned him that. If a teacher had, it would have come with a rubric and a due date and it would have become homework, and he probably would have done the minimum. Because it was his, he did way more than any assignment would have asked for.

The obvious objection is that students will pick something lazy. Some will. That's why the teacher's role doesn't disappear, it just changes. Instead of writing the assignment, the teacher approves the proposal. Before school ends in June, you turn in a page explaining what you want to do, what you'll produce at the end, and roughly how long it should take, and your teacher either signs it or sends it back for being too thin. "I'm going to read some books" gets rejected. "I'm going to read four novels by the same author and write about how her style changed" gets approved. That takes maybe ten minutes per student, and it keeps the standards while still letting the project belong to the person doing it.

There's also a point about what school is supposed to be preparing us for. In college and in almost any job, nobody hands you a packet. You're expected to notice something that needs doing, figure out how to do it, and manage your own time until it's done. Designing your own summer project is basically practice for that, and it's a skill you cannot build by following directions someone else wrote. My cousin, who is in her second year of college now, told me the hardest adjustment wasn't the difficulty of the classes but the fact that nobody was checking whether she'd started anything.

If summer projects are supposed to keep us learning, then they should be built to make us want to. Teacher-designed projects mostly teach students how to survive a packet. Student-designed projects, with a teacher holding the plan to a real standard, teach students how to start something and see it through, and that's worth more in September than six chapters of outlines nobody remembers.

Summer projects are one of those things almost nobody is happy about. Teachers assign them because they do not want us to forget everything by September, and students complain about them because summer is supposed to be the one part of the year that belongs to us. I actually think the projects are a fair idea. What schools get wrong is who designs them. Summer projects should be student-designed, with a teacher approving the plan, because students finish work they chose and because summer is the only stretch of time long enough to learn something the school year has no room for.

The first reason is the simplest one. People work harder on things they picked. Last summer my English class got a list of four novels and we had to choose one and write a five paragraph essay on its theme. I picked the shortest book, read it in two days in the middle of August, and wrote the essay the night before the first day of school. I could not tell you the main character's name right now. That same summer nobody assigned me anything about music, and I taught myself to read bass clef and learned somewhere around fifteen songs on my cousin's bass. The bass took maybe forty hours and the essay took four, and only one of them still exists in my head. When a project is handed to you, the goal quietly becomes finishing it. When you build the project yourself, the goal is the actual thing you are trying to do.

The second reason is that students' summers are not the same, and a single assignment pretends they are. My friend Dilara spends every summer working at her family's restaurant, basically from ten in the morning until closing. A teacher-designed project on, say, the causes of the First World War is just one more thing stacked on top of a fifty hour week for her, and she will do it badly at midnight. But if she were allowed to design it, she could track the restaurant's food costs for eight weeks, chart how the price of tomatoes moves, and figure out which dishes actually make money. That is real math and real economics, and she would be doing the work anyway. Meanwhile a kid going to a robotics camp could build something there and write it up, and a kid stuck home with nothing could finally read the six books he keeps saying he will read. One assignment cannot serve all three of them. Three plans can.

The obvious argument against this is that students would take the easy way out. Someone would propose "watch documentaries" and call it a summer of history. I think that is a real risk, but it is a risk about rules, not about who chooses the topic. The school can still set the requirements: a proposal turned in by the end of May, a minimum number of hours, some kind of evidence like a log or a draft or photographs, and a short presentation in September in front of an actual class. The teacher approves or sends the proposal back. That keeps the standards exactly where a teacher-designed project would put them, and it still leaves the subject to the student. And honestly, writing a proposal and defending it is a more useful skill than another theme essay, because that is what work looks like later.

Teachers should absolutely set the bar. They just should not pick the thing we jump over. Give us the requirements in May, make us plan it ourselves, and then make us show what we did. That is a summer project people might actually remember in October.

If schools are going to require summer projects at all, the projects should be designed by the students, with a teacher approving the plan and checking in.

The first reason is motivation, which is a boring word but it is really the whole thing. During the school year teachers have a lot of ways to make you do work. There are grades, there are due dates, there is the fact that you have to sit in the room with the person who assigned it, and there is the email that goes home. In the summer basically all of that disappears. The only thing left holding up a summer project is whether the student actually wants to do it, and a project someone else designed for a class of ninety kids is almost never the thing any particular one of those ninety kids wants to do. So you get compliance instead of learning. You get a reading log where the student read two chapters and guessed the rest, which is not what anybody was hoping for in June.

The second reason is that real summer learning is already happening, the packet just cannot see it. My friend Dev spent most of last July teaching himself to solder because he bought a broken guitar amp at a garage sale for eleven dollars and wanted to fix it. He watched probably forty hours of repair videos, he learned what a capacitor does and why you discharge one before you touch it, he ruined one board and then did not ruin the second one. Meanwhile his official assigned project was to read a novel and fill in a chart of literary devices, which he did on August 29th with the TV on. One of those two things was learning and one of them was paperwork, and the school only asked about the paperwork. If the assignment had been "propose something and show us what you did," Dev would have turned in something he was actually proud of, and probably would have talked about it for twenty minutes.

Third, designing your own project teaches a skill that a teacher-designed one cannot teach, which is how to plan work when nobody is standing over you. Nobody at a job hands you a worksheet with the steps already numbered. You have to decide what the goal is, guess how long it will take, be wrong about that, and adjust. Making an eleventh grader set a goal in June and then face in August what they actually did about it is uncomfortable, but it is a lot closer to how the rest of life works than a fill in the blank chart is.

The obvious objection is that some students will design themselves an easy summer. Somebody is going to propose "watch documentaries" and call it eight weeks of history. That is a fair worry, but it is an argument for approval, not for teachers designing everything. A one page proposal due in June with a goal, a rough plan, and a statement of what will be handed in lets a teacher write back "too vague, try again" before the summer even starts. There is also the case of AP classes, where the summer work is really prerequisite content you need on day one, like chemistry students reviewing dimensional analysis. I would keep that, but I would call it what it is, a short review assignment for one specific course, and not pretend it is a summer of learning.

Summer is the one stretch of time in a teenager's life where curiosity is not on a schedule. Schools should be careful about what they put into that space. Handing out ninety identical packets fills the space without using it. Asking each student what they want to learn, holding them to the plan they wrote, and then actually listening to what they made is harder to grade, but it is the only version of a summer project that has a chance of being worth the summer.
